Fix the swamp-adoption scaffold so extensions it generates earn the registry's license points.

Context: swamp 20261014.121640.0 (swamp-club#3324, commit 8dd0e86e in ~/src/swamp-club/swamp)
split the quality rubric's license check in two. `has-license` now needs a valid SPDX
`license:` in manifest.yaml. `license-file` needs a non-empty LICENSE/LICENSE.md in the
archive, listed as a bare basename under `additionalFiles:`. PR #491 in
webframp/swamp-extensions added `license: Apache-2.0` to every manifest in the repo and to
the five scripts/*-codegen generators. The swamp-adoption scaffold was deliberately left out
because it is published for other users, so hard-coding Apache-2.0 is wrong.

Today the scaffold (swamp-adoption/extensions/models/swamp-adoption/mod.ts, near the
`manifestVersion: 1` array around line 730) emits a manifest with no `license:` and, check
whether it emits a LICENSE file at all. Scaffolded extensions therefore score 92% (or lower)
and fail `swamp extension quality`.

Do:
1. Read CLAUDE.md (Licensing, Versioning, Release Notes, version-bump coupling rules) and
   load the swamp skill. Branch off origin/main in a worktree; PR #491 may or may not have
   merged yet, so check.

   with a small allow-list or format check; reject LicenseRef-*, since the rubric gives
   those no credit). Decide and document the default: either no default plus a clear
   warning in the output, or a documented placeholder. Do not silently default to
   Apache-2.0 for other users.

   emit a LICENSE.md stub listed in additionalFiles (or say plainly why not).

Base directory for this skill: /home/sme/.claude/skills/swamp

# Swamp

## Core Concepts

- **Models** — typed resource definitions exposing methods (create, stop,
  destroy, sync).
- **Data** — versioned state snapshots produced by method runs; referenced via
  CEL expressions.
- **Workflows** — declarative DAGs chaining model methods with guard expressions
  for idempotent execution and assert steps for validation.
- **Vaults** — secret storage referenced by models at runtime.
- **Extensions** — TypeScript packages adding model types, vault backends,
  datastores, reports, and webhook handlers.
- **Grants** — authorization rules for swamp serve access control.
- **Serve** — exposes the repo over the network with TLS and authentication.

## Routing Table

Route to the right guide based on what the user needs.

| User intent                                                   | Guide                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Models — create, run, edit, delete, search types              | [references/model/guide.md](references/model/guide.md)                         |
| Workflows — create, run, validate, DAG, history               | [references/workflow/guide.md](references/workflow/guide.md)                   |
| Data — list, query, versions, GC, delete                      | [references/data/guide.md](references/data/guide.md)                           |
| Vaults — create, store/read secrets, expressions              | [references/vault/guide.md](references/vault/guide.md)                         |
| Reports — run, configure, view, filter                        | [references/report/guide.md](references/report/guide.md)                       |
| Repository — init, upgrade, datastores, sources               | [references/repo/guide.md](references/repo/guide.md)                           |
| Extensions — create models/vaults/datastores/reports/webhooks | [references/extension/guide.md](references/extension/guide.md)                 |
| Publishing — push extensions to registry, deprecate           | [references/extension-publish/guide.md](references/extension-publish/guide.md) |
| Issues — file bugs, features, security reports                | [references/issue/guide.md](references/issue/guide.md)                         |
| Run tracking — active runs, stale detection, diagnostics      | [references/model/guide.md](references/model/guide.md)                         |
| Architecture — which primitive to use, design trade-offs      | [references/architecture/guide.md](references/architecture/guide.md)           |
| Sharing — promote solo repo to team, datastore + vault setup  | [references/share/guide.md](references/share/guide.md)                         |
| Serve — auth, grants, access control, tokens, OAuth           | [references/serve/guide.md](references/serve/guide.md)                         |
| Troubleshooting — errors, health checks, diagnostics          | [references/troubleshooting/guide.md](references/troubleshooting/guide.md)     |

## Common Commands

```bash
# Models
swamp model create <type> <name>               # create a model definition
swamp model @<type> method run <method> <name> # run a method on a model
swamp model get <name> --json                  # inspect current model state
swamp model type search [query]                # find available model types
swamp model list                               # list all models in the repo

# Data
swamp data list <name>                         # list data versions for a model
swamp data query '<CEL predicate>'             # query data with CEL expressions
# read one item's latest content (`swamp data get` is deprecated)
swamp data query 'model("<model>") && name == "<data>"' --select content

# Workflows
swamp workflow create <name>                   # create a new workflow
swamp workflow validate <name>                 # validate DAG before running
swamp workflow run <name>                      # execute a workflow
swamp workflow run <name> --input key=value    # execute with inputs
swamp workflow resume <name>                   # resume a suspended workflow
swamp workflow resume <name> --run <id>        # retry a failed run's failed steps
swamp workflow resume <name> --from <step>     # re-enter failed run at step
swamp workflow history search --json           # search run history

# Run tracking
swamp run history                              # recent runs (last 24h)
swamp run history --active                     # what's running right now?
swamp run doctor                               # diagnose stale/orphaned runs
swamp run doctor --fix                         # auto-reap stale runs

# Vaults, Reports, Extensions
swamp vault create <type> <name>               # create a vault for secrets
swamp report run <name>                        # run a report
swamp extension init <name>                    # scaffold a new extension
```

## Workflow

1. **Route** — match intent to a guide in the routing table.
2. **Load** — read the guide; load its `reference.md` if needed, deeper
   `references/` only when the guide says to.
3. **Validate** — before running any workflow: `swamp workflow validate <name>`.
   Before destructive methods (delete, stop, destroy):
   `swamp model get <name> --json` to confirm the target exists and is in the
   expected state. Proceed only when validation passes.
4. **Verify args** — run `swamp help <subcommand>` (e.g.
   `swamp help model method run`) to confirm exact flags and arguments before
   executing. The output is structured JSON — the canonical CLI schema.
5. **Execute** — run the command.
6. **On failure** — load
   [references/troubleshooting/guide.md](references/troubleshooting/guide.md)
   and diagnose before retrying or changing definitions.

## Rules

1. **Use the routing table, not memory.** Don't answer from cached knowledge
   about swamp commands — always load the current guide.
2. **Consult the architecture guide for design decisions.** Before choosing
   between primitives (model vs. workflow vs. extension vs. report) or
   explaining a design trade-off, load
   [references/architecture/guide.md](references/architecture/guide.md) and cite
   the design doc you relied on.
3. **Use swamp commands, don't go around them.** Query data with
   `swamp data query`, not by grepping `.swamp/` files. Interact with resources
   through model methods, not raw CLI tools when a model type already wraps the
   API — check with `swamp model type search`. Composing with `--json` output
   (e.g. piping through `jq`) is fine — the anti-pattern is bypassing swamp
   entirely.
4. **Verify flags with `swamp help` before executing.** `swamp help <command>`
   outputs the full CLI schema as structured JSON — every subcommand, argument,
   and option. Always run it to confirm exact flags before executing a swamp
   command (workflow step 4). Do not guess flags from memory.

# Pre-Push Review Loop

Run a local adversarial review on uncommitted or unpushed changes. Iterate
until the review passes, then stop and ask the human for push confirmation.

## When to Use

After making changes and before pushing to a remote branch. Especially
critical for:
- Fixes to prior adversarial review findings (regression risk is high)
- Concurrent-access code (locks, sequences, distributed state)
- Any change touching error handling or fallback paths
- New code (>200 LOC) — fresh code has too much surface area for a single pass

## The Loop

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                     │

## Phase 1: Show Diff

Collect the changes to review:

```bash
# Uncommitted changes against HEAD:
git diff HEAD

# Or unpushed commits against remote:
git diff origin/main...HEAD
```

Use whichever is appropriate. If there are uncommitted changes, review those.
If all changes are committed but unpushed, review the full branch diff.

## Phase 2: Run Quality Gates

Before sending to the reviewer, verify the code compiles and passes local
checks. This phase has two parts: standard gates and repo-specific gates.

### 2a. Standard Gates

Discover gates from the project's config files:

| Config file | Commands |
|-------------|----------|
| `deno.json` | `deno task check && deno task lint && deno task fmt:check && deno task test` |
| `package.json` | `npm run lint && npm run build && npm test` |
| `Cargo.toml` | `cargo check && cargo clippy && cargo test` |

If gates fail, fix them first. Do not send broken code to the reviewer.

### 2b. Repo-Specific CI Gates

Standard gates catch compile/lint/test failures. They do NOT catch structural
or convention failures that CI validates separately.

**Always check for repo-level guidance first.** Read steering files, skills,
CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, or contributing docs in the target repository. These
define what CI expects beyond standard compilation. Follow that guidance
exhaustively — run EVERY command listed, not a subset. Skipping a single
command from the checklist is the same as skipping Phase 2 entirely.

If no explicit guidance exists, fall back to these heuristics:

1. **Check CI workflow files** (`.github/workflows/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`).
   Identify validation steps beyond standard gates and run them locally.

2. **Compare directory structure against a peer.** In repos with many
   packages of the same kind, your new addition must match the structure
   of existing ones (marker files, metadata files, test file conventions).

3. **Run repo-specific validation commands locally.** If CI runs a
   validation command, run it yourself first.

**The principle:** if CI will run it, you run it first. "It compiled and
the tests passed" is necessary but not sufficient.

## Phase 3: Adversarial Review via Subagent

The subagent MUST have the same capability as a CI adversarial reviewer.
A diff blob with prose context is insufficient — the reviewer must read
the actual source files to trace execution paths, verify cross-function
consistency, and find protocol-level issues.

### Subagent Setup

Use a `general-task-execution` subagent. Provide:

1. **File paths to read** — tell the subagent which source files to read
   in full. The diff identifies *what* changed; the source files reveal
   *what interacts with* what changed. The subagent must read the complete
   implementation files, not just the diff.

2. **The diff** — for awareness of what's new vs existing code.

3. **Protocol and boundary context** — describe the external system's
   interface contract. For APIs: how input is parsed (line-delimited?
   shell-tokenized? JSON?). For CLI wrappers: how arguments are
   concatenated. For network protocols: framing, escaping, delimiters.
   The reviewer cannot find injection bugs without understanding the
   protocol boundary.

4. **Sibling consistency requirement** — if the code has multiple
   functions that do similar things (e.g., multiple command builders,
   multiple SSH invocations), explicitly instruct the reviewer to verify
   that ALL siblings apply the same validation/escaping/timeout patterns.
   Inconsistency between siblings is the #1 class of bug that single-pass
   reviews miss.

### Review Prompt Requirements

The subagent's review instructions MUST include these specific probes
(not just "assume broken"):

1. **Trace every interpolation site.** For each user-supplied value that
   ends up in a command string, network request, or file path: what
   characters can break the framing? Spaces, newlines, quotes, semicolons,
   pipes, backticks, dollar signs, null bytes — each has meaning in
   different contexts.

2. **Verify sibling consistency.** If function A validates input X, do
   ALL functions that accept the same class of input apply the same
   validation? List every sibling and confirm.

3. **Check timeout/resource bounds on every external call.** Every
   subprocess spawn, every network request, every fan-out: is there a
   hard deadline? What happens if it hangs? What happens if output is
   unbounded?

4. **Test with concrete breaking inputs.** For each finding, provide the
   exact input string that breaks it. "This could be a problem" is not a
   finding — "input X produces output Y which the server interprets as Z"
   is a finding.

5. **Verify the bootstrap/lifecycle path.** Can the code be invoked in
   the order the documentation describes? Are there circular dependencies
   between configuration and the methods that produce that configuration?

6. **Check truthiness vs nullability.** In JavaScript/TypeScript,
   `if (x)` skips `0`, `""`, `NaN`, `null`, `undefined`. For numeric
   parameters, `0` is often a valid value. For optional strings, `""`
   may be meaningful.

### Verdict Format

Require the subagent to produce:

```
### [CRITICAL|HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW] <title>
**File:** <path>
**Line(s):** <range>
**Issue:** What is wrong
**Breaking input:** The exact value that triggers the bug
**Impact:** What breaks
**Fix:** How to fix it

## VERDICT: PASS or FAIL
```

FAIL if any CRITICAL or HIGH findings exist. PASS otherwise.

## Phase 4: Evaluate Verdict

| Verdict | Action |
|---------|--------|
| PASS (no HIGH+) | Proceed to Phase 5 |
| FAIL (any HIGH+) | Fix findings, return to Phase 2 |

### On FAIL

- Fix ALL findings (HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW). Do not defer.
- After fixing, re-run quality gates (Phase 2)
- Re-run the adversarial subagent (Phase 3) on the CURRENT source files
- The re-review MUST re-read the source files — do NOT just re-review
  the new diff. Fixes often introduce new inconsistencies.
- Do NOT push between iterations

### Minimum Iterations

- For new code (>200 LOC of implementation): run at minimum 2 review
  iterations even if the first passes. Fresh code has too much surface
  area for a single pass to catch everything.
- For fixes to existing code (<50 LOC): one passing iteration is
  sufficient.

### Iteration Cap

Maximum 5 review iterations. If still failing after 5:
- Summarize what was fixed
- List remaining findings
- Ask the human for guidance — do not push in a failing state

## Phase 5: Ask to Push

When the review passes:

1. Show a brief summary of what changed
2. State: "Local adversarial review passed. Ready to push?"
3. **Wait for explicit human confirmation**
4. Only push after the human says yes

## Rules

- NEVER push without human confirmation, even on PASS
- NEVER skip Phase 2 (quality gates) — broken code wastes review cycles
- NEVER send only a diff to the reviewer — the subagent must read the
  full source files. A diff is supplementary context, not the primary input.
- NEVER defer a finding. Fix ALL findings before the next iteration.
  Deferral is not your decision — only the human can choose to ship with
  a known issue. If you think something should be deferred, ask
  explicitly. Otherwise, fix it.
- If the same finding appears twice across iterations, try a fundamentally
  different approach rather than tweaking the same fix
- After fixing findings, the re-review must check that the fix didn't
  introduce inconsistency with sibling code. Fixing function A without
  applying the same fix to sibling functions B and C is the most common
  regression pattern.
- The subagent review has confirmation bias limitations (it reads with
  fresher eyes than you, but still runs on the same model). Expect CI to
  occasionally catch things the local loop misses — but "occasionally"
  means one finding, not six rounds of fixes. If CI finds more than one
  HIGH after your pre-push loop, the loop was run incorrectly.

content.text:
The `scaffold` method now takes an optional `license` argument, and the independent adversarial review passed on its second round. Local `check`, `lint`, `fmt:check` and `test` (63 tests) pass. `swamp extension quality manifest.yaml` scores 13/13, 100%, with `has-license` and `license-file` both earned. The quality run used swamp 20261014.204224.0, newer than the required 20261014.121640.0. Nothing is pushed.

PR #491 had already merged, so I branched `feat/swamp-adoption-scaffold-license` off origin/main in the worktree `../swamp-extensions-scaffold-license`. It has three commits.

- **Validation:** `license` is an SPDX expression checked against a closed allow-list of common ids in exact case. It accepts `AND`, `OR`, `WITH` and parentheses. `LicenseRef-*`, unknown ids and any whitespace other than literal spaces are rejected. The same validation runs on the schema path and inside `execute`.
- **Default:** There is none. Without `license`, the scaffold logs a warning and emits no `license:`, no `LICENSE.md` and no `additionalFiles`. I put the warning after the design check, so a missing design fails on the design alone.
- **With a license:** The manifest gets `license: <spdx>` directly after `name:`, and `additionalFiles: [LICENSE.md]`. `LICENSE.md` is a placeholder that carries the id, a copyright line to fill in and a `TODO-REPLACE-LICENSE-TEXT` marker. It is not the full license text, because the scaffold can't ship arbitrary license texts. If someone publishes it unedited it still earns the `license-file` point, which the README and release notes both say. The generated `mod.ts` also gets a matching SPDX header.
- **Unrequested change:** The old template hard-coded `// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0` in every generated `mod.ts`. That header now appears only when a license is given.
- **Version bump:** To `2026.10.14.2` in the manifest and model, with an appended identity upgrade entry, a new `RELEASE_NOTES.md`, and a README note on the new argument. No exact-literal version assertion existed.
- **Tests:**
  - The `license:` line is present or absent as expected, and `LICENSE.md` is emitted only when a license is given.
  - Invalid values are rejected, covering `LicenseRef`, lowercase ids, malformed expressions and interior whitespace such as `\n` or NBSP.
  - Emitted values are canonical, with spaces collapsed.
  - The data name is `scaffold-current`, never `latest`.
- **Review round 1:** It found a HIGH bug. A newline inside `license` passed validation and corrupted the generated YAML manifest and `mod.ts`. I fixed it.
- **Review round 2:** It passed. I also fixed its five LOW findings, except that `WITH` is not tied to compatible licenses, so `MIT WITH Classpath-exception-2.0` is accepted. That is harmless to the rubric.
- **End-to-end check:** I generated a scaffold with `license=Apache-2.0` and ran the quality gate on it. It earned both license rows. Its other misses, README and symbol docs, are outside this task.
